It's incredibly frustrating, doctor, because I know I'm not a stupid man, but ever since that heart scare forced me into this chair, I just can't hold onto a thought to save my life.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time since you had to slow down due to your heart condition?\n\nPatient: Sad? Down? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, sure, it's frustrating as all get-out, having to sit around when I'm used to being on the go from sunup to sundown. It drives me absolutely up the wall, I'll admit that. But sad? Like, depressed? No, doctor, that's not it at all. \n\nI'm not sitting in my chair crying or feeling sorry for myself, if that's what you mean. I'm just... I'm just restless! It's like I have a motor running inside me that won't shut off, and nowhere to drive the car, you know what I mean? I'm agitated, I'm annoyed, I'm tapping my foot, I'm getting up to check the mail three times a day just to have something to do... but I'm not down in the dumps. I still want to do things, I still want to be out there fixing things and seeing folks. The desire hasn't gone anywhere. It's just my body—or I guess the doctors—telling me no, and then my brain deciding to take a vacation because it's bored. \n\nSo, no, I'm not sad. Just... well, just incredibly impatient with this whole slowing-down business, and annoyed that I can't seem to remember a darn thing while I'm doing it. I mean, just yesterday, my wife asked me to... well, anyway, no, I'm not feeling sad. Just restless. Very, very restless.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble focusing on tasks or conversations?\n\nPatient: Focusing? Oh, boy, yes. Yes, I do. And it's not just a little trouble, it's... well, it's becoming quite the issue, especially with the things I actually want to be doing, the things I enjoy! \n\nTake my bridge group, for example. I've been playing with these fellas for, gosh, it has to be going on fifteen years now. We used to meet up at the community center, but since my heart thing, they've been nice enough to come over to my place on Tuesday afternoons. Now, bridge is a game where you really have to pay attention, right? You have to track the cards, watch the bids, know what your partner is signaling. And I always prided myself on being sharp at the table. But lately? I can sit down at the bridge table, completely meaning to pay close attention, feeling totally ready for a good game, and then... I don't even know how it happens. After a little while, my mind just slides right off the game. I'll be looking at my cards, but I'm thinking about the gutters that need cleaning, or wondering if the mailman came yet, or just feeling this urge to stand up and stretch my legs. And suddenly, it's my turn to bid, and I realize I completely missed the last three plays and I have no earthly idea what's going on. The guys are starting to get a little annoyed with me, frankly, having to repeat themselves all the time.\n\nAnd it's the same thing with my Fix-It Friends group. We're this little bunch of retired guys in the neighborhood, we get together to plan out small repair projects for the older folks around here who can't do it themselves. We have these planning meetings, usually over coffee, to figure out who's bringing what tools and who's tackling which part of the job. I go into those meetings with a notepad, ready to focus, because it's important stuff! But, I swear, ten minutes into someone explaining how we're going to patch up Mrs. Higgins' back steps, my brain just... takes a walk. I'll be sitting right there, looking right at the guy talking, but I realize I just missed half of what was said. I have to lean over to my buddy Frank and whisper, \"Wait, are we using pressure-treated wood or not?\" It's embarrassing, doctor. I sit down fully intending to focus, but my attention just will not stay put. It just drifts away like a balloon you let go of.\n\nDoctor: Do you get any headaches or feel physically uncomfortable when you're trying to concentrate on something?\n\nPatient: Headaches? No, no, I wouldn't say I get headaches. I mean, my head feels fine. It's not a pain or an ache or anything like that when I'm trying to focus. And I don't feel sick to my stomach or dizzy or any of those things you might think of when you say \"physically uncomfortable.\" \n\nBut... well, uncomfortable is an interesting word, doctor, because I do feel... something. It's not a pain, like I said, but it's this... this awful, crawling sensation. Like when I was sitting at the bridge table last week—we were playing a particularly tricky hand, spades were trumps, and my partner had opened with a strong two clubs, which always requires a bit more mental math, you know? So I'm sitting there, really, really trying to bear down and concentrate on the cards that have been played, trying to remember if the jack of diamonds had come out yet. And the harder I tried to just sit still and focus my mind on that one specific thing, the more my body just... rebelled. \n\nIt starts in my legs, usually. This jittery, buzzing feeling, like I've got a hive of bees trapped right under my skin, right in my calves and my thighs. And it just builds and builds. It's not a headache, but it's this overwhelming physical urge that says, \"Get up! Move! Do something else!\" And if I try to ignore it and keep staring at my cards or keep listening to the Fix-It guys talk about Mrs. Higgins' steps, it moves up into my chest, this tight, restless energy. I start shifting in my chair, I cross my legs, I uncross them, I tap my fingers on the table... it's like my body is trying to physically escape the mental effort I'm putting in. \n\nSo, no, my head doesn't hurt. But trying to force myself to sit still and concentrate when my brain wants to drift off? It feels like trying to hold a beach ball underwater. It takes so much physical effort to fight that natural buoyancy, that urge to just pop back up to the surface and bounce around. It's exhausting, really, and it makes my whole body feel twitchy and impatient. But no actual pain or headaches, no. Just that terrible, restless buzzing.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your weight since you started having these memory and focus issues?\n\nPatient: Weight? Oh, well, let me think about that for a second. You know, you'd think with all this... this sitting around I'm supposed to be doing, I'd be putting on the pounds left and right. My wife, she certainly worries about it. Ever since the cardiologist told me to take it easy, she's been watching my plate like a hawk, making sure I'm not overdoing it on the salt or the butter or whatever the latest thing we're not supposed to eat is. \n\nAnd honestly, I'm in the kitchen half the day anyway! Not because I'm hungry, mind you, but just because I can't sit still in that recliner for more than twenty minutes. I get up, I wander into the kitchen, I open the refrigerator door, stare at the mustard and the leftover meatloaf for a minute, close it, open the pantry, look at the crackers... I'm just pacing, really. Just looking for something to do with my hands. Sometimes I'll grab a handful of peanuts just for the crunch, just to have an activity, you know? \n\nBut even with all that pacing and snacking and hanging around the kitchen driving my wife absolutely crazy—she tells me I'm going to wear a groove right through the linoleum if I keep it up, I swear—my weight hasn't actually changed a bit. I step on that old scale we have in the master bathroom, the one with the dial that you have to tap with your toe a few times to make sure it's at zero before you get on it? We bought that thing at Sears back in the nineties, I think. Anyway, I step on that every Sunday morning, regular as clockwork, and the needle just sits right there at 185, same as it has for the last five years. \n\nSo, no, despite the heart thing and the pacing and the memory stuff making me forget if I even ate breakfast sometimes... well, no, the weight itself hasn't gone up or down. It's just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself feeling extremely sleepy during the day?\n\nPatient: Sleepy? Oh, gosh, no. No, not at all. It’s actually quite the opposite, if you can believe it. My wife, she’s always telling me, she says, \"Why don't you just sit down and take a nap? You're retired now, you've earned a rest, especially with the heart doctor telling you to take it easy.\" And I look at her like she's speaking Greek! Sleepy? I don't even know what it feels like to want to close my eyes in the middle of the afternoon. \n\nI try, you know. I really do try, mostly just to make her happy. I'll go get in that big brown leather recliner we have in the den—the one right in front of the television, very comfortable chair, we've had it forever—and I'll put on a golf tournament or maybe one of those old Westerns. You know, something slow-paced, thinking, \"Okay, I'll just doze off for twenty minutes like normal retired folks do.\" But... well, my eyes just stay wide open. I’m laying back, and instead of drifting off, my brain is just going a mile a minute, and my legs start doing that twitching thing I was telling you about earlier. That awful buzzing feeling just creeps right back in. \n\nAnd before I know it, I haven't been in the chair five minutes and I'm up again, walking around, checking the thermostat, looking out the front window to see if the neighbor is mowing his lawn, wandering back into the kitchen to stare at the pantry shelves again. I just have too much of this... this nervous energy, I guess you'd call it. It's like my engine is just idling too high all day long, just humming away, and I can't find the switch to turn it off. \n\nSo, no, sleepy isn't the word at all. If anything, I almost wish I *could* feel a little sleepy during the day, just to get a break from feeling so wound up and restless all the time. It might be nice to actually get some peace and quiet in my own head for half an hour! But a daytime nap? No, doctor, that's just not in the cards for me. Never happens.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting irritable or short-tempered more often than you used to?\n\nPatient: Irritable? Short-tempered? Well, let me think about that. You know, I really wouldn't say so. I've always been a pretty easygoing sort of fellow, and I don't think that's changed much. If anything, it's the people around me who seem to be getting short-tempered with *me*! My wife, for instance, bless her heart, she gets so frustrated with me when we're out and about. \n\nJust the other day—I think it was Tuesday, because that's when the garbage goes out and I had noticed the wheel on the big green bin was getting a bit wobbly—anyway, we were down at the hardware store. Miller's Hardware, over on 4th Street, not one of those giant warehouse places, I always prefer the local guys because they actually know where the bolts are. I just needed a couple of washers and maybe some of that heavy-duty grease. Well, we get up to the front, and they only had one register open. The fellow in front of us was trying to return a ceiling fan that he'd clearly already tried to install, had the wires all stripped and everything, and he was arguing with the poor cashier, just holding up the whole line. \n\nNow, someone who's short-tempered, they might start huffing and puffing, right? Maybe muttering under their breath, getting mad at the cashier or the guy with the fan. But me? I wasn't angry at all. I wasn't irritable. I just... I couldn't just stand there in that line while they hashed the whole thing out. I mean, my feet literally wouldn't let me just stand on that hard concrete floor for ten minutes doing nothing. And then I wandered over to the garden hoses, and then I was looking at the new snow shovels—which is ridiculous because it's the middle of the warm season—but I just had to keep moving, just to give my hands and feet something to do. \n\nBy the time I finally looped back around to the register, my wife was practically steaming, asking me where on earth I went and why I couldn't just stand still in a line for five minutes like a normal person. She was the one who was irritable! But me? I was perfectly fine. I just have that... that constant need to be doing something. It's not anger. It's not a temper thing at all. I don't yell at people or get snappy. I just sort of... buzz away, you know? \n\nI suppose I might walk away from a conversation if it's dragging on too long, or I might interrupt somebody because I just can't hold a thought in without blurting it out, but it's never because I'm mad at the person talking. It's just that my engine is running too fast and I've decided it's time to move on to the next thing. So, no, doctor, no real temper to speak of. Just a whole lot of pacing.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself having trouble expressing your thoughts in a coherent or orderly way?\n\nPatient: Expressing my thoughts? Coherent? Well, gosh, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble with that. I mean, I know exactly what I want to say, and I say it. If anything, I probably express my thoughts a little *too* much! My wife would certainly agree with that. \n\nJust this past Sunday, I was on the phone with my older brother, Frank. Anyway, I was explaining to Frank exactly how I took the carburetor apart, step by step, how you have to be careful with the float bowl gasket because they dry out and crack so easily, and how I soaked the jets in cleaner overnight. \n\nI had the whole process perfectly lined up in my head, very orderly. Oh, heavens, yes. This isn't exactly a new development, doctor. I mean, if you were to ask my poor mother—God rest her soul—she'd tell you I came into this world kicking and talking and I just never really stopped. \n\nEven way back as a boy in grade school, it was exactly the same story. I remember, oh, it must have been third grade. Mrs. Higgins' class. We had those old wooden desks, you know the ones? With the heavy metal runners on the bottom and the little groove at the top where your pencil would sit, and the seat was attached right to the desk behind you. The other kids would have their hands raised, sitting nice and quiet like little angels, but the answer was already out of my mouth before my arm even thought about going up. It was like a reflex. I just got so excited that I knew it, the words just tumbled out. \n\nI got in so much trouble for that. The notes she used to send home... oh, boy. My mother had a whole stack of them in the kitchen drawer. Always the same thing: \"He’s a bright boy but he talks too much,\" or \"He disrupts the other students,\" or \"He simply will not stay seated.\" Sometimes, if it was a really bad day, they used to fold the note up and pin it right to my winter jacket so I couldn't accidentally \"lose\" it on the walk home. \n\nSo, yes, this... this buzzing engine I was telling you about? It's been running hot since I was in short pants. It’s never been out of malice or trying to be a bad kid, it’s just always been how I'm wired, I suppose. Just a whole lot of energy with nowhere to put it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any recreational drugs or misused prescription medications?\n\nPatient: Recreational drugs? Oh, gosh, no. No, no, no. I've never been one for any of that business. You know, back when I was a younger man, coming out of high school in the early seventies... well, you can imagine, there was a whole lot of that sort of thing going around. People smoking this and taking that, especially when I got my first job working down at the old lumber yard. Just a cup of black coffee in the morning, and that's about all the substance I need to get my engine running for the day!\n\nDoctor: Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or attention deficit disorder when you were younger?\n\nPatient: A diagnosis? Oh, heavens no. No, they didn't have any of those fancy terms back when I was coming up. \n\nI mean, I'm sixty-eight years old, doctor. I don't think that was even a thing people went to doctors for back then! If you couldn't sit still, they didn't send you to a clinic, they sent you straight to the principal's office. Mr. Abernathy, that was his name. Big, tall man, always wore these heavy wool suits even in the springtime, smelled like Old Spice and peppermint. He'd sit me down in this hard wooden chair right outside his door and tell me I just needed to \"apply myself\" and \"settle my spirit.\" Settling my spirit! Ha! That was my mother’s favorite phrase. \"He’s just got ants in his pants, he can't help it.\" Or the teachers would make you stay after school to clap the chalk erasers together out by the chain-link fence until your hands and your corduroys were just coated in white dust. We didn't see a doctor for anything unless it was strep throat or a broken bone. I did break my arm once, actually, falling out of the old oak tree behind the Methodist church because I thought I could swing from one branch to another like Tarzan, but... well, that's a whole different story. He'd sit me down in this hard wooden chair right outside his door and tell me I just needed to \"apply myself\" and \"settle my spirit.\" Settling my spirit! Ha! As if I could just flip a switch and turn the engine off.\n\nBack then, they just called you a chatterbox, or a handful, or they said you had ants in your pants. That was my mother’s favorite phrase. \"He’s just got ants in his pants, he can't help it.\" Or the teachers would make you stay after school to clap the chalk erasers together out by the chain-link fence until your hands and your corduroys were just coated in white dust. I must have clapped ten thousand erasers in my time, just trying to burn off that extra energy. \n\nSo, no, no doctor ever put a label on it. We didn't see a doctor for anything unless it was strep throat or a broken bone. I did break my arm once, actually, falling out of the old oak tree behind the Methodist church because I thought I could swing from one branch to another like Tarzan, but... well, that's a whole different story. But as for my brain and the way I act? No, nobody ever diagnosed me with anything like that. I was just considered a boy with too much motor and not enough steering wheel.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience any of these symptoms, such as difficulty sitting still or paying attention, when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Well, I—like I was saying just a little bit ago, doctor, maybe I got a little carried away with my stories earlier and didn't make it clear enough, but yes, absolutely. It's funny you bring it up again because... well, it really was just my whole childhood in a nutshell. \n\nEven as a boy in grade school, I was always the kid who just couldn't stay in his seat. Not for love or money! I'd be up, wandering around, looking out the window at the custodian mowing the lawn, or tapping my pencil on the desk until the kid next to me wanted to scream. And I blurted out answers left and right. I just couldn't hold them in, the words would just fly out of my mouth before the teacher even finished asking the question. \n\nAnd like I mentioned with those notes... I got so many notes sent home just for talking too much and not staying put. My poor mother, she actually kept them in this old wooden cigar box on top of the refrigerator, right next to the spare fuses and the scotch tape. She'd pull another one out of my pocket—or unpin it from my jacket, like I was telling you—and just shake her head and sigh. She must have had fifty of those little slips of paper in that box by the time I hit middle school. So, yes, that difficulty sitting still and keeping my attention focused where it belonged, it's been with me since the very beginning.\n\nDoctor: Have your memory and focus issues, or your restlessness and impulsivity, caused any problems for you at work, or in your relationships with family and friends?\n\nPatient: Well, now, as far as work goes, I’ve been retired for a few years now, so I don't have a boss breathing down my neck anymore, thank the good Lord. But... well, I suppose it has been causing some friction, yes. \n\nI volunteer down at the community senior center—we have this little repair group, just a bunch of us old-timers fixing up broken toasters and wobbly chairs and whatnot for folks in the neighborhood. It keeps the hands busy, you know? But, I have to admit, it’s gotten to where the senior-center repair group can’t really count on me the way they used to. I’ll go in there with all the best intentions to fix Mrs. Gable's standing fan, but then I'll see a radio with a frayed wire, or someone will bring in a grandfather clock, and before I know it, I’ve got three different appliances taken apart on my workbench, screws and springs everywhere, and the whole afternoon is just gone. Bob—he’s the fellow who organizes the whole thing, nice guy, wears those thick glasses—he’s had to pull me aside a couple of times because people are asking for their things back and I just... I jump from one project to the next and don't finish the first one. It makes me feel terrible, honestly, because I really do want to help, I just get so sidetracked by whatever's right in front of me.\n\nAnd it's not just the repair group, either. It’s bleeding over into my personal life, especially with my own appointments. My wife tries her best to keep me on the straight and narrow, like with that pill organizer I told you about, but she can't manage every single thing for me. Just recently, my regular doctor’s office has had to chase me—literally call the house two or three times—about missed heart follow-ups. I’m supposed to go in and get these routine checks, and they'll hand me the little appointment card, and I think to myself, \"Okay, I'll go home and put this right on the corkboard in the kitchen.\" \n\nBut then I step out of the clinic, maybe run into an old buddy from the lumber yard, or decide I need to swing by the hardware store for some sandpaper, and poof! The card ends up at the bottom of the washing machine in my pants pocket, and I completely miss the day. Then Brenda from the front desk is calling, and my wife is giving me that look... you know the look. I feel like maybe I'm losing my mind, or maybe you're just testing my memory to see if I'm paying attention! Because, like I was just telling you a few minutes ago, yes, absolutely. I feel like a bit of a broken record here, but even as a boy in grade school, I was exactly that kid. \n\nI was the one who just couldn’t stay in his seat to save his life. I'd be up and wandering, and I always blurted out answers before the poor teacher could even finish her sentence. From the time I was just a little fellow, I was bouncing around, speaking out of turn, getting those little slips of paper pinned to my coat... it's never really stopped. It just changed from school desks and chalk erasers to workbenches and broken toasters. My wife loves going to those Sunday matinees down at the old theater in town—they show the classic films, you know, the ones we grew up with, and they have those nice plush seats. She just wants to relax and eat her popcorn, but I can barely make it through the opening credits without moving. When I’m sitting there, even if I'm trying my absolute hardest to just focus on the screen, my foot is just going a mile a minute. Up and down, up and down, bouncing on the sticky floor. \n\nAnd if we're at a table, like when Bob calls one of our planning meetings for the senior center repair group—which, honestly, we don't need a whole hour just to figure out who's fixing what, but Bob loves his printed agendas—my fingers are always tapping the table. It drives the other fellows half mad. Or I’ll grab whatever's sitting right in front of me. I'll be turning a pen around and around in my hand, flipping it end over end, clicking it, taking the cap off and putting it back on. \n\nThe funny thing is, doctor, I don't even realize I'm doing it!
